record.paper_title: A survey of open questions in adaptive therapy: bridging mathematics and clinical translation
record.context_brief: Necessary model conditions for delaying resistance
record.original_question: For adaptive cancer therapy, understood as dynamic patient-specific dose modulation or dose timing that maintains treatment-sensitive tumor cells so they competitively suppress treatment-resistant tumor cells, what cancer and model conditions are necessary for adaptive therapy to delay treatment resistance? In particular, when resistance is costly, resistant cells can be suppressed by competition with sensitive cells, and therapy reduces sensitive cells, what objectives should define therapeutic success, and do conclusions from simple sensitive/resistant-cell models remain valid when real-tumor components such as healthy cells, immune cells, resources, Allee effects, and phenotypic plasticity are included?

evidence.quote: 1.1 What are the necessary conditions for adaptive therapy to delay resistance?

It is thought that the success of adaptive therapy in delaying the emergence of resistance depends on three characteristics of the cancer: a) resistance is costly, b) resistant cells can be suppressed by competition with sensitive cells, and c) therapy reduces the population of sensitive cells.

These simple models raise two further questions: 1) what are the appropriate objectives for evaluating the success of therapy? 2) do the main results hold up in models that include additional components of real tumors?

With the exception of the success of high dose therapy with a strong Allee effect, no universal therapy can achieve all three objectives of lowering average dose, delaying time to emergence of resistant cells, and reducing total tumor burden.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Consider adaptive cancer therapy, defined as dynamic, patient-specific modulation of drug dose or dose timing that deliberately preserves a population of treatment-sensitive tumor cells in order to competitively suppress treatment-resistant tumor cells and thereby delay therapeutic failure. Model a tumor as a population (or interacting collection of populations) of sensitive cells S(t) and resistant cells R(t), evolving under a controllable therapy schedule u(t). It is commonly hypothesized that adaptive therapy delays the emergence of resistance when three conditions hold: (a) resistance carries a fitness cost in the absence of therapy, (b) resistant cells are suppressed by competition with sensitive cells, and (c) therapy reduces the population of sensitive cells.

Address the following questions rigorously.

1. Determine the precise set of conditions on a sensitive/resistant tumor model and its therapy protocol that are necessary, and the set that are sufficient, for adaptive therapy to delay the emergence of resistance compared with standard continuous maximum-tolerated-dose therapy. In particular, formalize and assess whether conditions (a)–(c) above are each necessary.

2. Propose and justify an appropriate definition of therapeutic success. Specifically, examine the three candidate objectives: (i) lowering the time-averaged therapeutic dose, (ii) delaying the time to emergence/expansion of resistant cells, and (iii) reducing total tumor burden over the treatment horizon. Decide whether any single therapy protocol can simultaneously optimize all three objectives, or whether trade-offs are unavoidable.

3. Investigate whether the conclusions drawn from minimal two-compartment sensitive/resistant models remain valid when the model is augmented to include additional realistic components of tumors, including: healthy (non-cancerous) host cells, immune cell populations interacting with the tumor, shared limiting resources (such as oxygen, nutrients, or space), Allee effects (positive density dependence at low population sizes), and phenotypic plasticity allowing reversible switching between sensitive and resistant states. Identify which of these mechanisms preserves, modifies, or invalidates the conditions identified in (1) and the conclusions of (2).
artifact.status_search_result: The question is posed as an open research direction in a 2022/2023 survey on adaptive therapy. Partial answers exist: Strobl et al. (Cancer Research, 2021) show that a resistance cost is not strictly necessary when tumors are near carrying capacity and resistance is rare, and identify four key modulating factors (initial resistant fraction, proximity to carrying capacity, resistant proliferation rate, turnover). Subsequent works (2024–2025) on treatment-pausing thresholds and stochastic/deterministic cycle stability further refine the conditions. However, a complete characterization of necessary/sufficient conditions across extended models (immune, healthy cells, Allee, plasticity) and a unifying notion of therapeutic success remain unresolved.

status_evidence.title: Turnover Modulates the Need for a Cost of Resistance in Adaptive Therapy
status_evidence.snippet: A resistance cost is not necessary for adaptive therapy to extend time to progression if the tumor is close to carrying capacity and resistance is rare.
status_evidence.claim: Condition (a) (cost of resistance) is not strictly necessary, partially answering question 1.

status_evidence.title: Conditional success of adaptive therapy: treatment-pausing thresholds
status_evidence.snippet: Conditional success of adaptive therapy revealed by mathematical modeling of treatment-pausing thresholds.
status_evidence.claim: Further refinements of conditions for success continue to appear, indicating ongoing partial progress.
